# Sacubitril/Valsartan in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Heart failure (HF) remains a major global health burden, affecting more than 60 million people worldwide and imposing substantial morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs [1]. For decades, the cornerstone of pharmacological therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) centered on inhibition of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system (RAAS) and beta-adrenergic blockade [2]. The advent of sacubitril/valsartan, the first-in-class angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI), represented a paradigm shift in the management of HFrEF [3].

## Mechanism of Action

Sacubitril/valsartan is a supramolecular sodium salt complex combining the neprilysin inhibitor prodrug sacubitril (AHU377) with the angiotensin II receptor blocker valsartan [4]. Neprilysin is a neutral endopeptidase that degrades several vasoactive peptides, including natriuretic peptides, bradykinin, and adrenomedullin [5]. By inhibiting neprilysin, sacubitrilat (the active metabolite) augments levels of natriuretic peptides, promoting natriuresis, diuresis, vasodilation, and inhibition of maladaptive cardiac remodeling [6]. Simultaneously, valsartan blocks the angiotensin II type 1 receptor, counteracting the deleterious vasoconstriction and sodium retention that would otherwise result from concomitant angiotensin II accumulation [7]. This dual mechanism distinguishes ARNI from earlier attempts at combined neprilysin–ACE inhibition, which were abandoned because of unacceptable angioedema risk [8].

## Pivotal Clinical Evidence in HFrEF

The landmark PARADIGM-HF trial established sacubitril/valsartan as superior to enalapril in symptomatic HFrEF [9]. In this randomized, double-blind study of 8,442 patients, sacubitril/valsartan reduced the composite of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization by 20% and lowered all-cause mortality compared with enalapril, prompting early termination for benefit [9]. Subsequent analyses demonstrated reductions in sudden cardiac death and progression of disease [10], as well as benefit across the spectrum of baseline risk [11]. Health-related quality of life and symptom burden also improved [12]. These results led to rapid incorporation into international guidelines as a replacement for ACE inhibitors or ARBs in eligible patients [2,13].

The TRANSITION and PIONEER-HF studies extended the evidence base to patients hospitalized with acute decompensated HF [14,15]. PIONEER-HF demonstrated that in-hospital initiation produced a greater reduction in NT-proBNP than enalapril, with a favorable safety profile [15]. These findings supported earlier initiation rather than waiting for outpatient stabilization [16].

## Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction

The role of ARNI in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is more nuanced. The PARAGON-HF trial randomized 4,822 patients with ejection fraction ≥45% and narrowly missed its primary endpoint of total HF hospitalizations and cardiovascular death [17]. However, prespecified subgroup analyses suggested potential benefit in patients with lower ejection fraction (below the normal range) and in women [18]. A pooled analysis of PARAGON-HF and PARADIGM-HF reinforced the concept of treatment benefit declining with increasing ejection fraction [19]. These data informed an expanded, ejection fraction–dependent indication, particularly for patients with mildly reduced ejection fraction [20].

## Safety and Tolerability

Sacubitril/valsartan is generally well tolerated. The most common adverse effects are hypotension and hyperkalemia, with the former more frequent than with enalapril and the latter less frequent [9]. Angioedema occurred infrequently but mandates avoidance of concomitant ACE inhibitor use and a 36-hour washout when switching [21]. Renal function and serum potassium require monitoring, although renal outcomes were favorable relative to enalapril [22]. Theoretical concerns regarding neprilysin inhibition and amyloid-beta accumulation prompted cognitive studies, with the PERSPECTIVE trial showing no significant adverse cognitive effect over three years [23].

## Implementation and Special Populations

Despite robust evidence, real-world uptake of sacubitril/valsartan has been suboptimal, with therapeutic inertia, cost, and tolerability concerns contributing to underutilization [24]. Registry data demonstrate that many eligible patients remain on conventional RAAS inhibitors or receive suboptimal dosing [25]. Initiatives promoting rapid sequencing of the four foundational HFrEF therapies—ARNI, beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and SGLT2 inhibitors—advocate early ARNI introduction [26]. Cost-effectiveness analyses have generally supported its value, particularly given reductions in costly hospitalizations [27]. Data also suggest beneficial effects on reverse cardiac remodeling, with reductions in left ventricular volumes and improvements in ejection fraction [28]. Benefits appear consistent across age groups, diabetic status, and renal function strata [29].

## Conclusion

Sacubitril/valsartan has transformed contemporary heart failure care, offering mortality and morbidity benefits beyond conventional RAAS inhibition in HFrEF and a more selective role in HFpEF and mildly reduced ejection fraction [30]. Ongoing efforts should focus on improving implementation, optimizing dosing, and clarifying its role across the ejection fraction spectrum.
